title: I need to scale my system
summary: From a vague scaling problem to the topology, platform, traffic and observability decisions that follow if you split into services.

steps.why: Start by naming the kind of scaling you need: traffic, data or team. The answer decides whether a topology change helps at all.
If the bottleneck is team coordination rather than one saturated resource, the topology question comes up.
A move to microservices introduces service-to-service communication concerns: every function call becomes a network call.
Service-to-service communication introduces service discovery requirements, because instances come and go as services scale and redeploy.
Kubernetes provides orchestration and service discovery within its ecosystem, which is why many teams evaluate it at this point.
External traffic entering a Kubernetes environment introduces ingress and routing considerations.
API gateways add API management and traffic control (authentication, rate limits, versioning) on top of routing.
Distributed systems increase the importance of observability: a single request now crosses many processes.
OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral way to produce the metrics, logs and traces observability depends on.
Distributed tracing helps engineers understand request flows across services and find where latency comes from.
Reliability engineering provides the principles and practices needed to manage the resulting system.

title: My infrastructure costs are increasing
summary: Turn a rising bill into unit costs, then decide where managed services, compute models and offloading help.

steps.why: First decide what level of performance you are paying for and whether it is worth it.
A rising bill is only a problem if cost per customer or per request is rising. Measure that.
Compare managed premiums with the staff time self-managed components really cost.
Idle capacity is a common waste; the compute model decides whether you pay for it.
Offloading traffic to a CDN often lowers both latency and origin cost.
Egress-heavy storage is a frequent hidden cost driver.

title: My database is becoming a bottleneck
summary: The usual order of database scaling levers, from cheapest to hardest to undo.

steps.why: Removing repeated reads is usually the cheapest way to reduce database load.
If reads still dominate, replicas add read capacity with SQL semantics, at the cost of replication lag.
Replicas and caches are eventually consistent; decide which reads must hit the primary.
If writes are the bottleneck, understand why multi-primary is rarely the answer.
When one primary cannot take the write load, partitioning is the next step.
Know how sharding goes wrong before choosing a shard key.
For known access patterns at extreme scale, a horizontally scalable database may fit better than sharding.

title: My system has reliability issues
summary: Set a target, find single points of failure, contain cascades, then plan recovery and verify it.

steps.why: Agree what availability the business needs before spending on it.
Express the target as SLOs so you can tell when you are missing it.
Find the components, dependencies and people whose failure alone causes an outage.
Most large outages are small faults that spread; understand how.
Retries hide transient faults but must be bounded to avoid amplifying load.
Fail fast on dependencies that are already failing, so callers survive.
For site-level failures, choose a multi-site strategy that matches your recovery objectives.
Verify the design by injecting failures deliberately.

title: My deployment process is becoming complicated
summary: Decide the compute model and orchestration level, avoid premature Kubernetes, then pave the path for teams.

steps.why: Start with the packaging and compute model; it sets everything else.
With containers, decide whether you need a general orchestrator.
Recognize the signs that Kubernetes would cost more than it saves.
On AWS, compare against a simpler managed orchestrator.
When many teams repeat the same deployment work, a platform may pay off.
Make the right deployment path the easiest one.

title: My engineering team is struggling with service ownership
summary: Connect team structure to system structure and fix ownership before splitting further.

steps.why: System boundaries tend to mirror team boundaries; start there.
Recognize the symptoms of components without owners.
Decide where infrastructure responsibility lives.
Avoid replacing unclear ownership with a central queue.
Ownership boundaries do not always need deployment boundaries.

title: How should I handle asynchronous communication?
summary: From sync vs async to brokers, failure handling and whether Kafka is warranted.

steps.why: Decide which interactions can complete later.
The simplest async pattern: absorb bursts with a queue.
When many consumers react to the same facts, events replace point-to-point calls.
Every async flow needs somewhere for failing messages to go.
Decide whether replay and fan-out justify a streaming platform.
Check the signs that a simpler queue is enough.
Compare broker models directly.
